question: In many theatres it is considered bad luck to whistle backstage, and the rule has a very practical origin, not a magical one. What was the original danger behind this superstition?
correct_answer: Whistles were cues for lowering scenery
alternative_answers: Stagehands used whistles as rigging signals
A stray whistle could drop scenery on someone
Sailor stagehands cued scene changes by whistling
Whistling accidentally triggered a scenery change
It could cause sandbags or sets to be dropped
Whistles signalled the fly crew to move scenery
headline_answer: Whistles were cues for lowering scenery
topic: Dance, theatre and the performing arts
source_excerpt: sailors, and by extension theatrical riggers, used coded whistles to cue scene changes.

extra.verification_notes: Standard account: sailor-trained stagehands used whistle cues for flying scenery, so stray whistling risked dropping scenery on people (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatrical_superstitions).

explanation: Before electronic cue systems, backstage riggers were often former sailors, hired because they knew how to handle ropes and pulleys. They borrowed the ships' habit of signalling with coded whistles, so a whistle backstage told the crew to raise or lower a piece of scenery or a sandbag counterweight. An actor whistling idly in the wings could therefore trigger a heavy set piece being dropped from the fly loft onto someone's head. The ban on whistling started as a safety rule and survived as a superstition long after the whistle cues disappeared.

question: Which crime writer's whodunnit has been playing in London's West End since 1952, making it the longest-running play in the world?
source_excerpt: by far the longest run of any play in the world

extra.why_interesting: Players know Christie as a novelist; few realise her stage whodunnit has outlasted every other play in history and is still selling tickets.
extra.verification_notes: The Mousetrap by Agatha Christie opened in 1952 and is still running in the West End in 2026, the longest run of any play in the world (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mousetrap).

explanation: The Mousetrap has clocked up tens of thousands of performances, and every audience is still asked not to reveal the killer on the way out.

question: Which street-born dance style made its Olympic debut at the Paris 2024 Games, only to be dropped again for Los Angeles 2028?
source_excerpt: the sport is not slated for inclusion at the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles

extra.why_interesting: A dance from Bronx block parties became an Olympic sport, then vanished again after a single Games.
extra.verification_notes: Breaking debuted at Paris 2024 and is not on the LA 2028 programme (baseball/softball, cricket, flag football, lacrosse, squash were added instead); I found no reinstatement.

explanation: Breaking got exactly one Olympics, with judges scoring b-boys and b-girls in head-to-head battles on the Place de la Concorde.

question: Cirque du Soleil, now a global touring empire, was founded in 1984 by a troupe of street performers in which country?
source_excerpt: founded on June 16, 1984, in Baie-Saint-Paul, Quebec by former street performers Guy Laliberté and Gilles Ste-Croix

extra.why_interesting: The French name sends many players to France; the answer is a Canadian stilt-walker's street troupe.
extra.verification_notes: Cirque du Soleil was founded in 1984 in Baie-Saint-Paul, Quebec, Canada by former street performers Guy Laliberté and Gilles Ste-Croix; nothing newer contradicts this.

explanation: It started in the small Quebec town of Baie-Saint-Paul, where co-founder Guy Laliberté had been working as a fire-eater and stilt-walker.

question: The Moulin Rouge cabaret opened in Paris in 1889, the same year the city unveiled which landmark built for its World's Fair?
source_excerpt: constructed as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair

extra.why_interesting: Two icons of Paris, the cabaret and the tower, were born in the same year, which few players have ever connected.
extra.verification_notes: Moulin Rouge opened 6 Oct 1889 and the Eiffel Tower was the centrepiece of the 1889 Paris World's Fair, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower.

explanation: Paris got its tower in March and its can-can palace in October of the same year, and both were expected to be temporary novelties.

question: Riverdance was born as a seven-minute interval act during the 1994 edition of which televised contest, hosted that year in Dublin?
source_excerpt: Riverdance began as an interval act during the Eurovision Song Contest 1994... a seven-minute segment

extra.why_interesting: A seven-minute filler slot while the votes were counted became a stage show seen by tens of millions worldwide.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Riverdance began as a seven-minute interval act at Eurovision 1994 at the Point Theatre, Dublin.

explanation: Michael Flatley and Jean Butler filled the gap while the votes came in, and the interval act upstaged every song in the competition.

question: Which French king earned his famous nickname partly by dancing the role of the rising sun in a court ballet at the age of 14?
source_excerpt: King Louis XIV appears with the coming of the day as the sun god Apollo, one of his many personifications as the rising sun

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the Sun King nickname came from grandeur or propaganda; it came in part from a teenage ballet costume.
extra.verification_notes: Louis XIV, born 1638, danced the rising sun/Apollo in Ballet Royal de la Nuit (1653) at age 14, which matches the Sun King nickname.

explanation: Louis was a serious dancer who later founded the Royal Academy of Dance, which is why ballet steps are still named in French today.

question: The name of Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre is simply the Russian word for what?
source_excerpt: The name 'Bolshoi' translates to 'Large' or 'Big' in Russian; Большой театр (Bol'shoy teatr) literally means 'Large Theater.'

extra.why_interesting: A name that sounds grand and mysterious to foreigners turns out to be the plainest description possible.
extra.verification_notes: Bolshoi (Большой) means 'large/big' in Russian; no name change or newer event affects this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolshoi_Theatre).

explanation: It is literally the Big Theatre, and its neighbour across the square is the Maly, which just means the Small Theatre.

question: True or false: Kabuki, the Japanese theatre form in which every role is played by a man, was founded by a woman.
source_excerpt: Izumo no Okuni is credited as kabuki's founder... women were banned from performing in kabuki theatre in 1629

extra.why_interesting: An art form famous for its all-male casts was invented by a woman, which flips the player's expectation completely.
extra.verification_notes: Kabuki is credited to Izumo no Okuni, a woman, and was later restricted to male performers (yarō-kabuki) after the 1629 ban; minor modern exceptions don't undermine the irony. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabuki

explanation: A shrine dancer named Izumo no Okuni started kabuki in Kyoto around 1603, and the all-male tradition only began when the authorities banned women from the stage in 1629.

question: In 2009, UNESCO added the tango to its cultural heritage list after a joint bid by Argentina and which neighbouring country?
source_excerpt: Inscribed in 2009 (4.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity

extra.why_interesting: Everyone files tango under Argentina alone; the dance actually grew up on both banks of the Río de la Plata.
extra.verification_notes: UNESCO's page confirms Argentina and Uruguay jointly submitted tango, inscribed in 2009, with no later change in status.

explanation: Tango grew up in the port districts of both Buenos Aires and Montevideo, so the two countries applied together rather than fight over it.

question: Which Stravinsky ballet, choreographed by Nijinsky, provoked a near-riot at its Paris premiere in 1913?
source_excerpt: Many have called the first-night reaction a 'riot' or 'near-riot'

extra.why_interesting: Ballet is imagined as polite and genteel; this premiere had the audience shouting and brawling in the stalls.
extra.verification_notes: Rite of Spring, choreographed by Nijinsky, premiered in Paris on 29 May 1913 amid uproar; the 'near-riot' label is standard, though the article notes it only came into use with 1924 reviews.

explanation: The pounding rhythms and stamping, turned-in choreography so enraged the audience that Nijinsky had to shout counts to the dancers from the wings.

question: Three of these famous ballets have music by Tchaikovsky. Which one does not?
source_excerpt: a romantic ballet (ballet-pantomime) in two acts with music by Adolphe Adam.

extra.why_interesting: All four are staple classical ballets that sound like one family; the player must know that one of them predates Tchaikovsky's ballet career entirely.
extra.verification_notes: Giselle's music is by Adolphe Adam, while Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker are Tchaikovsky's (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giselle).

explanation: Giselle was written by the French composer Adolphe Adam in 1841, some 35 years before Tchaikovsky's first ballet, Swan Lake.

question: In The Nutcracker, which keyboard instrument, so new that Tchaikovsky had one quietly shipped from Paris, gives the Sugar Plum Fairy's dance its bell-like sound?
source_excerpt: the Variation de la Fée Dragée (commonly known as the Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy)

extra.why_interesting: The most familiar tinkling melody in ballet was a brand-new sound at the time, and the composer treated the instrument like a trade secret.
extra.verification_notes: Celesta is correct: Tchaikovsky used it in the Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy. The Paris-shipment detail is from memory and not confirmed by the fetched page.

explanation: Tchaikovsky asked his publisher to keep the purchase secret so that Rimsky-Korsakov and Glazunov would not beat him to using the new instrument.

question: In which year did the city of Strasbourg suffer its notorious dancing plague, when dozens of people danced in the streets for days on end?
source_excerpt: July to September 1518 in Strasbourg, Alsace

extra.why_interesting: The player must place a bizarre mass event in time; each distractor is a famous disaster year that feels equally plausible for a 'plague'.
extra.verification_notes: The Strasbourg dancing plague occurred in July–September 1518, per Wikipedia; no dispute about the year.

explanation: It began in July 1518 with a single woman dancing in the street, and within a month dozens had joined her, some reportedly dancing until they collapsed.

question: The whirling dervishes of Turkey belong to a Sufi order founded by followers of which 13th-century Persian poet?
source_excerpt: The order was established after Rumi's death in 1273 by his son Sultan Veled and Husameddin Chelebi

extra.why_interesting: A poet whose lines fill modern greeting cards is the spiritual founder of a spinning dance ritual that still draws crowds in Turkey.
extra.verification_notes: The Mevlevi Order (whirling dervishes) was established after Rumi's death in 1273 by his son Sultan Veled and Husameddin Chelebi, so Rumi is correct.

explanation: The Mevlevi order was established in Konya after Rumi's death in 1273, and the spinning ceremony is a form of moving meditation in his memory.

question: Speaking at Gettysburg in 1863, Abraham Lincoln began with 'Four score and seven years ago'. Which year was he counting back to?
source_excerpt: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.

extra.why_interesting: The archaic phrasing sounds like poetry, but it is just a sum: 1863 minus 87 lands on the founding year any adult can name.
extra.verification_notes: Four score and seven (87) years before 1863 is 1776, the Declaration of Independence, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettysburg_Address.

explanation: A score is twenty, so four score and seven is 87 years, which takes 1863 back to 1776 and the Declaration of Independence.

question: Which US president stood at the Brandenburg Gate in 1987 and demanded, 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'?
source_excerpt: Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!

extra.why_interesting: Players know the line but often blur the speaker with Kennedy's earlier Berlin speech; the answer separates the two Cold War moments.
extra.verification_notes: Reagan delivered the 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' speech at the Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987; this is historical and can't be superseded.

explanation: Reagan made the challenge in June 1987, and the Berlin Wall fell just over two years later, in November 1989.

question: In which 1939 film does Rhett Butler walk out with the words, 'Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn'?
source_excerpt: Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn.

extra.why_interesting: One of cinema's most quoted exits, and the player only needs to recall the film it closes.
extra.verification_notes: Gone with the Wind (1939) contains Rhett Butler's line 'Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn' per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gone_with_the_Wind_(film).

explanation: Clark Gable delivered the line to Vivien Leigh's Scarlett O'Hara, and the mild curse caused a stir with Hollywood's censors at the time.

question: 'Play it again, Sam' is never said in Casablanca. Which character actually asks Sam to play 'As Time Goes By'?
source_excerpt: Ilsa says, "Play it once, Sam, for old time's sake. Play it, Sam. Play 'As Time Goes By.'"

extra.why_interesting: Everyone pictures Bogart's Rick growling the request, but the famous ask actually comes from Ilsa.
extra.verification_notes: Ilsa asks Sam to 'Play it, Sam. Play As Time Goes By'; Rick never names the song, and 'Play it again, Sam' is never said (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_it_again,_Sam).

explanation: It is Ingrid Bergman's Ilsa who says 'Play it, Sam', while Humphrey Bogart's Rick later only snaps 'Play it!'

question: True or false: the line 'Elementary, my dear Watson' appears in Arthur Conan Doyle's original Sherlock Holmes stories.
source_excerpt: the phrase 'Elementary, my dear Watson' is never uttered in any of the sixty stories by Conan Doyle.

extra.why_interesting: The line is the detective's signature in popular memory, yet Conan Doyle never wrote it.
extra.verification_notes: The phrase never appears verbatim in Conan Doyle's sixty stories, so 'False' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherlock_Holmes).

explanation: Holmes says 'Elementary' on its own in one story, but the full catchphrase was coined by later stage plays and films.

question: Recalling the first atomic bomb test, physicist Robert Oppenheimer quoted 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.' From which ancient Hindu scripture does that line come?
source_excerpt: Oppenheimer recalling his thoughts after witnessing the Trinity test

extra.why_interesting: The line sounds like it was written for the atomic age, but it is a Hindu scripture more than two thousand years old.
extra.verification_notes: The line is Oppenheimer's translation of Bhagavad Gita 11.32, which he recalled in later interviews; Wikipedia confirms his Gita association and the Trinity recollection video (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Oppenheimer).

explanation: Oppenheimer had studied Sanskrit and took the words from the Gita, where the god Vishnu reveals his cosmic form.

question: Caesar's boast 'I came, I saw, I conquered' followed a lightning victory in 47 BC. In which modern country was that battle fought?
source_excerpt: Near Zile in the Tokat province of northern Turkey

extra.why_interesting: Players picture Caesar in Gaul or Rome, but the boast was earned in Anatolia against a king of Pontus.
extra.verification_notes: Battle of Zela (47 BC), after which Caesar said 'veni, vidi, vici', took place near Zile in modern Turkey.

explanation: The Battle of Zela was fought in Pontus, in what is now northern Turkey, against King Pharnaces the Second, and it was over in a few hours.

question: In November 1973 Richard Nixon told newspaper editors, 'I am not a crook.' At which famous Florida resort was that press conference held?
source_excerpt: On November 17, 1973, the Contemporary Resort was the site of ... Nixon declared, "I am not a crook."

extra.why_interesting: A grim Watergate denial is imagined in the White House, but it was delivered at a theme park resort.
extra.verification_notes: Nixon's Nov 17, 1973 APME press conference, where he said 'I'm not a crook', was held at Disney's Contemporary Resort in Walt Disney World, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney%27s_Contemporary_Resort

explanation: Nixon spoke at the Contemporary Resort hotel at Disney World near Orlando, and resigned less than a year later.

question: Which New York Yankees star, forced to retire by the disease that now bears his name, told a stadium crowd in 1939 that he was 'the luckiest man on the face of the earth'?
source_excerpt: I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth.

extra.why_interesting: A dying athlete calling himself the luckiest man alive is the inversion that makes the speech immortal; the disease now carries his name.
extra.verification_notes: Gehrig gave the 'luckiest man on the face of the earth' farewell speech at Yankee Stadium on July 4, 1939, after his ALS diagnosis; ALS is commonly called Lou Gehrig's disease.

explanation: Gehrig gave his farewell speech at Yankee Stadium on the fourth of July 1939, and ALS is still widely known as Lou Gehrig's disease.

question: British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain promised 'peace for our time' after returning from Munich with Hitler's signature. In which year?
source_excerpt: I believe it is peace for our time...

extra.why_interesting: The phrase is famous as a byword for failed appeasement; pinning it to the Munich year tests whether the player knows how close it came to the war.
extra.verification_notes: Chamberlain delivered the 'peace for our time' remarks on 30 September 1938 after Munich, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Chamberlain spoke outside Downing Street in September 1938, and Germany invaded Poland less than a year later.

question: In August 1940 Churchill said 'never was so much owed by so many to so few'. Who were 'the Few' he was praising?
source_excerpt: airmen of the Royal Air Force (RAF) and aviators of the Fleet Air Arm, Royal Navy who fought in the Battle of Britain

extra.why_interesting: The sentence is universally known, but players must connect it to the specific airmen Churchill meant, not soldiers or sailors.
extra.verification_notes: 'The Few' are Battle of Britain airmen, chiefly RAF Fighter Command pilots; the answer is the standard one but slightly narrow, since Bomber and Coastal Command crews were also included (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Few).

explanation: He meant the Royal Air Force pilots fighting the Battle of Britain, who were holding off the Luftwaffe that summer.

question: At the 1963 March on Washington, which gospel singer is credited with shouting 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!', nudging Martin Luther King to abandon his prepared text?
source_excerpt: Mahalia Jackson shouted "Tell 'em about the dream, Martin!"

extra.why_interesting: The 'dream' passage was not in the script; a singer's shout from behind him is credited with pulling it out.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's 'I Have a Dream' article credits Mahalia Jackson with the shout; Branch's doubt that King heard her doesn't contradict the 'credited with' wording.

explanation: Jackson had performed just before King spoke, and her shout is credited with turning a solid speech into the 'I Have a Dream' moment.

question: 'Let them eat cake' is pinned on Marie Antoinette, but the line already appeared in the memoirs of which Geneva-born philosopher, written when she was still a child?
source_excerpt: The first six books were written in 1765 and published in 1782. Marie Antoinette was nine years old when Rousseau wrote it in 1765.

extra.why_interesting: The quote defines Marie Antoinette in popular memory, yet it was already in print when she was a young girl.
extra.verification_notes: Rousseau's Confessions (books written 1765) contain the 'let them eat brioche' anecdote when Marie Antoinette was about nine; Rousseau was Geneva-born. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let_them_eat_cake

explanation: Rousseau's Confessions attributes the remark to an unnamed 'great princess', and there is no evidence Marie Antoinette ever said it.

question: Which British ocean liner was torpedoed by a German submarine off the coast of Ireland in 1915, helping turn American opinion against Germany?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: The sinking killed 128 US citizens and significantly increased American public support for entering the war

extra.why_interesting: Players know a liner was sunk by a U-boat in the First World War but often blur it with Titanic; the stem's date and submarine lock it to one famous name.
extra.verification_notes: Lusitania was torpedoed by U-20 off the Old Head of Kinsale, Ireland, on 7 May 1915, and the sinking turned American opinion against Germany.

explanation: The Lusitania went down in about eighteen minutes, and nearly 1,200 people died, including more than a hundred Americans.

question: In the Pirates of the Caribbean films, what is the name of the ship Captain Jack Sparrow spends the first movie trying to win back?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: Barbossa mutinied against and marooned [him] on a deserted island... Jack is determined to reacquire the Black Pearl

extra.why_interesting: A warm-up everyone can reach; the fun is in remembering that Jack spends most of the first film trying to get the ship back rather than sailing it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's plot summary confirms Sparrow spends the first film trying to reacquire the Black Pearl, which Barbossa took in a mutiny.

explanation: The Black Pearl had been stolen by his mutinous first mate Barbossa, which is why Jack starts the film with no ship at all.

question: The cruise ship Costa Concordia capsized in 2012 after striking rocks just off a small island belonging to which country?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: the cruise ship deviated from her planned route at Isola del Giglio, Italy in order to perform a sail-by salute, and as a consequence struck a rock formation

extra.why_interesting: The images of a giant liner lying on its side next to a tiny island were everywhere; the name of the ship itself nudges players toward the right Mediterranean country.
extra.verification_notes: Costa Concordia struck rocks off Isola del Giglio, Italy, on 13 January 2012, per Wikipedia; this is a fixed historical fact.

explanation: She ran aground off Giglio in Tuscany, and the wreck lay on its side in plain view of the island's harbour for more than two years before being refloated.

question: Which English sea captain, denounced as a pirate by Spain, was knighted by Queen Elizabeth the First on the deck of his own ship, the Golden Hind?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: Queen Elizabeth awarded Drake a knighthood aboard Golden Hind in Deptford on 4 April 1581; the dubbing being performed by a French diplomat, Monsieur de Marchaumont.

extra.why_interesting: The man Spain called a pirate was knighted by his own queen on the deck of the very ship he had used to raid Spanish treasure.
extra.verification_notes: Drake was knighted aboard the Golden Hind in 1581 by Elizabeth's award (the physical dubbing was by a French envoy) and Spain branded him a pirate; the answer is unambiguous. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Drake

explanation: Drake had just sailed around the world and returned with a hold full of plundered Spanish silver, so the queen came to Deptford in 1581 to reward him in person.

question: When the pirate 'Calico Jack' Rackham was captured in 1720, two members of his crew turned out to be women. Name either of them.
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: Rackham, Bonny, and a crew including another woman, Mary Read, stole the merchant sloop William.

extra.why_interesting: The idea of women fighting on a pirate deck in the 1700s still surprises people, and their story is one of the best documented in the whole era.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Rackham's 1720 capture with two women crew, Anne Bonny and Mary Read, so Anne Bonny is correct.

explanation: Both women escaped hanging by telling the court they were pregnant, and one of them reportedly scolded Rackham that if he had fought like a man he need not have died like a dog.

question: Which ship raced through the night to rescue the roughly 700 survivors sitting in the Titanic's lifeboats?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: rescued over 700 survivors from the ship's lifeboats

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the ship that sank; far fewer can name the one that steamed through ice fields all night to pick up the people in the boats.
extra.verification_notes: Carpathia raced through the night and rescued over 700 survivors from Titanic's lifeboats, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The Carpathia's captain, Arthur Rostron, pushed his ship past its normal top speed through the ice to arrive at dawn, and was later honoured in both Britain and America.

question: Gordon Lightfoot's hit 'The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald' tells of a huge freighter lost with all 29 crew in 1975 on which body of water?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: sank in Lake Superior during a storm on November 10, 1975, with the loss of the entire crew of 29 men.

extra.why_interesting: A player assumes a famous shipwreck song is about the ocean; the twist is that a 220-metre freighter vanished with all hands on a lake.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Edmund Fitzgerald sank in Lake Superior on Nov 10, 1975 with all 29 crew, matching the question and answer.

explanation: The Fitzgerald was over 220 metres long, yet a November storm on the largest of the Great Lakes sank her so fast that no distress call was ever sent.

question: Tom Hanks played the captain of which container ship, hijacked by Somali pirates in 2009 and later freed by US Navy snipers?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: two US Navy SEAL Team Six snipers of Red Squadron and one USAF CCT from the 24th STS fired shots from Bainbridge's fantail, killing the three remaining pirates.

extra.why_interesting: Players remember the Tom Hanks film but usually only the captain's name; the ship's name is the proud near-miss that reveals who really followed the news story.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Tom Hanks played Capt. Richard Phillips of Maersk Alabama, rescued by Navy SEAL snipers in 2009; later renaming to MV Tygra doesn't change the answer.

explanation: The real Captain Richard Phillips spent five days as a hostage in a lifeboat before SEAL marksmen on a nearby destroyer ended the standoff with three shots.

question: Alexander Selkirk, the real-life castaway who inspired Robinson Crusoe, spent four years marooned on a Pacific island that today belongs to which South American country?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: Más a Tierra, located in the uninhabited Juan Fernández archipelago 670 km (420 mi) off the coast of Chile.

extra.why_interesting: Readers place Crusoe on a Caribbean island; the real castaway sat on a Pacific island off South America, and a player who knows it is Pacific can reason their way to the country.
extra.verification_notes: Selkirk was marooned on Más a Tierra (now Robinson Crusoe Island) in the Juan Fernández archipelago, which belongs to Chile; the roughly four-year duration matches (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Selkirk).

explanation: The island lies about 670 kilometres off the Chilean coast, and Chile officially renamed it Robinson Crusoe Island in 1966 to cash in on the connection.

question: Killed in a fight off the coast of North Carolina in 1718, the pirate Edward Teach is far better known by what nickname?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: Edward Teach (or Thatch; c. 1680 – 22 November [3 December N.S.] 1718), better known as Blackbeard, was an English pirate

extra.why_interesting: Players know the nickname instantly but almost nobody knows the ordinary man behind it; the plain surname Teach makes the legend feel suddenly human.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Edward Teach, better known as Blackbeard, was killed at Ocracoke Inlet, North Carolina, in 1718; the spelling variants of his surname don't affect the answer.

explanation: Teach reportedly tied slow-burning fuses into his beard before battle so smoke curled around his face, and his whole piratical career lasted barely two years.

question: Which Swedish warship sank on its maiden voyage in 1628 after sailing little more than a kilometre, and today fills its own museum in Stockholm?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: The ship sank after sailing roughly 1,300 m (1,400 yd) into her maiden voyage on 10 August 1628.

extra.why_interesting: A flagship built to dominate the Baltic never left its own harbour; the player expects a wreck story at sea and gets one that ends within sight of the shipyard.
extra.verification_notes: Vasa sank on its maiden voyage on 10 August 1628 after about 1,300 m and is housed in the Vasa Museum in Stockholm (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasa_(ship)).

explanation: A gust tipped the top-heavy ship over in front of the crowds, and after more than three centuries in the cold, low-salt water it was lifted almost intact in 1961.

question: Found drifting in the Atlantic in 1872, seaworthy and with its cargo of alcohol still aboard but not a soul on deck, which ship became the world's most famous ghost ship?
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: dishevelled but seaworthy condition under partial sail

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes a 'ghost ship' is folklore; this one was a real, documented vessel whose crew simply vanished with the ship still perfectly sailable.
extra.verification_notes: Mary Celeste was found adrift 4 Dec 1872, seaworthy with 1,701 barrels of alcohol aboard and crew missing; no later developments change this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Celeste).

explanation: The crew's single lifeboat was missing and the ship's papers were gone, yet the vessel sailed on for about ten days with nobody at the wheel, and no trace of the people was ever found.

question: True or false: in the early 1800s, a pirate fleet of tens of thousands of men on the coast of China was commanded by a woman.
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: the fleet consisted of approximately 400 junks and between 40,000 and 70,000 pirates.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture pirate chiefs as Caribbean men like Blackbeard; the largest pirate force in history was Chinese and commanded by a woman, who also negotiated an amnesty and died in peace.
extra.verification_notes: Zheng Yi Sao led the Red Flag Fleet, a confederation of tens of thousands of pirates, off the coast of China from 1807 to 1810 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zheng_Yi_Sao).

explanation: Zheng Yi Sao took over her late husband's Red Flag Fleet and led it against the Qing navy, then negotiated a pardon that let her retire and die peacefully in her sixties.

question: Robert Ballard's famous 1985 expedition that found the Titanic was officially a cover story. What had the US Navy really sent him to inspect on the Atlantic floor?
alternative_answers: the wrecks of Thresher and Scorpion
topic: Shipwrecks, pirates and the high seas
source_excerpt: The Navy directed Ballard to find two nuclear-powered attack submarines that had sunk in the 1960s: the USS Scorpion and the USS Thresher.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume finding the Titanic was the whole point of the famous 1985 expedition. In fact it was the side project: the US Navy only paid for it so Ballard could secretly check on two lost Cold War nuclear subs, and the Titanic hunt got the leftover days.
extra.verification_notes: Navy's real mission was surveying the wrecks of nuclear subs USS Thresher and USS Scorpion, per the Washington Times report on Ballard's 2008 disclosure; no newer events change this.

explanation: The Navy wanted the wrecks of the lost subs USS Thresher and USS Scorpion checked for radiation leaks and clues to their sinking, and only after that job was done did Ballard get about twelve days to hunt for the Titanic.

question: A train's two wheels on one axle are fixed together, so they must spin at exactly the same rate. Yet on a curve the outer rail is longer than the inner one. How does a train get round a bend without one wheel skidding?
correct_answer: Cone-shaped wheels roll on different diameters
alternative_answers: Tapered wheel treads act like a differential
The axle shifts sideways so the outer wheel rolls on a bigger circumference
Wheels are wider at the flange so the outer one uses a larger diameter
headline_answer: Cone-shaped wheels roll on different diameters
source_excerpt: when one wheel is pushed closer to the adjacent (outer) rail, it presents a bigger circumference to the rail than when centred on the track.

extra.verification_notes: Standard explanation: conical wheel treads let the outer wheel roll on a larger diameter than the inner on curves (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_wheel).

explanation: Railway wheels are not flat cylinders but slightly cone-shaped, wider near the inside flange and narrower at the outer edge. On a curve the whole axle slides a little toward the outside of the bend, so the outer wheel rides on its fat part and the inner wheel on its thin part. Spinning at the same rate, the outer wheel now covers more ground per turn than the inner one, exactly what the longer outer rail needs. The axle effectively steers itself, and the flanges only touch the rail as a last resort on very tight curves.

question: The curving stone viaduct that the Hogwarts Express crosses in the Harry Potter films is a real railway bridge. In which country?
source_excerpt: The viaduct is built on a curve of 792 feet (241 m).

extra.why_interesting: The curved viaduct looks like a fantasy set, but it is a working 19th-century railway bridge that tourists can ride a real steam train across today.
extra.verification_notes: Glenfinnan Viaduct, a curved stone railway viaduct in Lochaber, Scotland, appears in the Harry Potter films as the Hogwarts Express route.

explanation: It is the 21-arch Glenfinnan Viaduct on the West Highland Line, and a real steam train still crosses it every summer with fans leaning out of the windows.

question: The longest perfectly straight stretch of railway track in the world runs for 478 kilometres across a flat, treeless plain. On which continent?
source_excerpt: longest straight stretch of railway track in the world... 478.193 kilometres (297.135 miles)

extra.why_interesting: Players assume railways always curve around something; here there is nothing to curve around for nearly 500 km.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 478 km straight section on the Trans-Australian Railway across the Nullarbor Plain, Australia; no newer record found.

explanation: It crosses the Nullarbor Plain, whose Latin-derived name literally means no trees, and the Indian Pacific train takes several hours to cover the straight without a single bend.

question: In which year did Japan's first bullet train line, from Tokyo to Osaka, carry its first passengers?
source_excerpt: The Tokaido Shinkansen opened on October 1, 1964, connecting Tokyo to Shin-Ōsaka, in time for the 1964 Summer Olympics.

extra.why_interesting: Most players place high-speed rail in the 1980s or later; Japan was running 210 km/h bullet trains while the Beatles were still together.
extra.verification_notes: Tokaido Shinkansen (Tokyo–Osaka) opened on October 1, 1964, which matches the claimed answer; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokaido_Shinkansen

explanation: The line opened just nine days before Tokyo hosted the Summer Olympics, showing the world a Japan rebuilt and racing ahead at 210 km/h.

question: In 1869 a golden spike was hammered in to join the two halves of America's first coast-to-coast railroad. In which US state did the rails meet?
source_excerpt: Promontory Summit marks the site where the First Transcontinental Railroad was completed May 10, 1869, from Omaha to Sacramento

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the coast-to-coast line to have been joined somewhere dramatic like California or the Rockies, not in a remote Utah desert.
extra.verification_notes: The golden spike joined the Union Pacific and Central Pacific at Promontory Summit, which is now in Utah (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promontory_Summit); Utah was a territory in 1869, which is a negligible nuance.

explanation: The ceremony took place at Promontory Summit near the Great Salt Lake, and the journey from New York to San Francisco shrank from months to about a week.

question: The longest railway tunnel in the world opened in 2016 and runs for 57 kilometres beneath a mountain range. Which country built it?
source_excerpt: Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland remains the world's longest conventional railway tunnel at 57,104 m, opened in 2016.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for the Channel Tunnel or something in Japan; the record holder is a flat route bored straight through the Alps.
extra.verification_notes: Gotthard Base Tunnel (Switzerland, opened 2016, ~57 km) remains the world's longest railway tunnel per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_tunnels.

explanation: The Gotthard Base Tunnel lets trains cross the Alps on an almost flat track, and it beat Japan's Seikan Tunnel to the record by several kilometres.

question: Until 2018, every long-distance train timetable across Russia, even in Vladivostok seven hours ahead, showed times according to the clock of which single city?
source_excerpt: Russia announced it would stop running all long-distance trains across its 11 time zones on Moscow time, ending a frequent cause of confusion for travellers.

extra.why_interesting: The Trans-Siberian crosses seven time zones, yet for over a century a passenger in Vladivostok reading a departure board was looking at a clock set thousands of kilometres away.
extra.verification_notes: Russian long-distance trains ran on Moscow time until Aug 2018, when local time replaced it; Vladivostok is +7h from Moscow (https://www.france24.com/en/20180725-russian-trains-end-dependence-moscow-time).

explanation: Russian Railways ran its whole network on Moscow time, so a Trans-Siberian passenger might board at what the timetable called four in the morning while the sun was high overhead.

question: The railway to Lhasa in Tibet climbs above 5,000 metres. What do its carriages pump in for passengers that no other ordinary train needs to?
source_excerpt: each seat in the train is equipped with an oxygen supply outlet for any possible emergency.

extra.why_interesting: Players think of a train as the gentle way to travel; here the route is so high that the carriages need equipment normally associated with hospitals or aircraft.
extra.verification_notes: Qinghai–Tibet Railway reaches 5,072 m and its carriages have oxygen enrichment and per-seat oxygen outlets; no newer development found that overturns this.

explanation: The line crests the Tanggula Pass at 5,072 metres, where the air is so thin that the sealed carriages are enriched with oxygen and have outlets by the seats.

question: Which city's famous railway terminal, with 44 platforms stacked on two underground levels, has more platforms than any other station in the world?
source_excerpt: Grand Central covers 48 acres (19 ha) and has 44 platforms, more than any other railroad station in the world.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the record in a rail-mad country like Japan, Germany or China; the answer is a commuter terminal in a city most associate with the subway.
extra.verification_notes: Grand Central Terminal in New York has 44 platforms on two underground levels, the most of any station; no newer record found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Central_Terminal).

explanation: Grand Central Terminal hides its platforms beneath the celebrated main concourse, and all of them are dead ends serving commuter trains rather than long-distance routes.

question: Named after a water bird, which British steam locomotive set the world speed record for steam at 203 km/h in 1938, a record never beaten?
source_excerpt: 126 mph (203 km/h)

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a 1930s record would have fallen long ago; steam was abandoned before anyone bothered to beat it, so a duck-named engine remains champion.
extra.verification_notes: Mallard's 126 mph (203 km/h) on 3 July 1938 remains the officially recognised steam speed record; no newer record found per Wikipedia.

explanation: Mallard hit the mark on a downhill stretch near Grantham, and since steam engines vanished from mainlines in the following decades, nobody ever came back to challenge it.

question: In Agatha Christie's most famous railway mystery, a snowdrift traps the Orient Express and its passengers overnight. In which country, as it was then called, does the train come to a halt?
source_excerpt: caught far beyond Vinkovci station in Yugoslavia (today Croatia)

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the train gets stuck in snow, but almost nobody thinks about where; the glamorous express is stranded in the Balkans, not the Alps.
extra.verification_notes: The novel places the snowbound train in Yugoslavia, beyond Vinkovci (now Croatia), so the answer is correct as the country was then called.

explanation: Christie strands the train between Vinkovci and Brod in what is now Croatia, giving Hercule Poirot a sealed carriage full of suspects and nowhere for the killer to run.

question: Australia's famous Ghan train crosses the continent from Adelaide to Darwin. Its name honours which group of people who travelled that route long before the rails did?
source_excerpt: may honor Afghan camel drivers who arrived in Australia in the late 19th century to help the British colonists find a way to reach the country's interior.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect an Australian outback train to be named after an explorer, a town or an animal; the answer reveals that camels and the men who drove them from Afghanistan and the Indian subcontinent were the original transport of the interior.
extra.verification_notes: The Ghan's name derives from 'The Afghan Express', commonly said to honour the Afghan camel drivers; the route is still Adelaide–Darwin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ghan).

explanation: Camel trains led by cameleers known collectively as Afghans supplied the outback in the nineteenth century, and the railway that replaced them was nicknamed the Afghan Express, soon shortened to the Ghan.

question: For centuries, one chess piece could move only a single square diagonally. Around 1500 its powers exploded and it became the strongest piece on the board. Which piece?
source_excerpt: Initially, its only move was one square diagonally.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the queen was always the monster of the board; in fact for centuries she was nearly the weakest piece on it.
extra.verification_notes: The queen's predecessor, the fers, moved one square diagonally and gained modern queen powers in the late 15th century, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(chess).

explanation: The medieval queen was a feeble adviser shuffling one diagonal square at a time; the sudden upgrade was so dramatic that Europeans nicknamed the new game 'mad queen chess'.

question: The famous 12th-century chess pieces carved mostly from walrus ivory, with wide-eyed kings and shield-biting warriors, were discovered in 1831 on an island belonging to which country?
source_excerpt: discovered in 1831 on the Isle of Lewis in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland

extra.why_interesting: Walrus ivory and Viking-style carving suggest Scandinavia, and the pieces were probably made in Norway, but they were dug out of a sand dune on a windswept Hebridean island.
extra.verification_notes: The Lewis chessmen were found in 1831 on the Isle of Lewis, Outer Hebrides, Scotland; the Norwegian origin of the pieces does not change which country the island belongs to now.

explanation: They are the Lewis chessmen, found on the Isle of Lewis in the Outer Hebrides, and they later starred as the wizard chess set in the first Harry Potter film.

question: Two black aces and two black eights are known in poker as the dead man's hand. Which Wild West gunfighter was shot from behind in Deadwood in 1876 while supposedly holding them?
source_excerpt: was shot in the back of the head by Jack McCall.

extra.why_interesting: The 'dead man's hand' is pub-trivia famous, but far fewer people can name the actual gunfighter whose last cards it describes.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Wild Bill Hickok was shot in the back of the head by Jack McCall in Deadwood on 2 Aug 1876 and is the figure associated with the dead man's hand; the question's 'supposedly' covers the disputed cards.

explanation: James Butler 'Wild Bill' Hickok uncharacteristically sat with his back to the door and was shot in the head by Jack McCall mid-game.

question: In which casino card game is the best possible hand an ace plus a ten-value card, dealt as your first two cards?
source_excerpt: A total of 21 on the starting two cards is called a 'blackjack' or 'natural,' and is the strongest hand.

extra.why_interesting: A gentle warm-up: the description is enough for anyone who has ever played a casino card game.
extra.verification_notes: Blackjack's natural (ace plus ten-value card as the first two cards) is the strongest hand per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackjack; variants like pontoon are forms of the same game.

explanation: That two-card 21 is called a natural and usually pays out at three to two, better than any other winning hand in the game.

question: Add together every number from 1 to 36 on a roulette wheel. What notorious total do you get?
source_excerpt: Is the sum of all the numbers on a roulette wheel (0 through 36). This is a corollary of the fact that the number is a Triangular number

extra.why_interesting: A quick mental sum, or a vague memory of the casino legend, lands the player on a number with a devilish reputation.
extra.verification_notes: 1+2+...+36 = 36*37/2 = 666, and Wikipedia confirms the roulette-wheel sum is 666 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/666_(number)).

explanation: The sum is 666, which is why roulette has long been called 'the devil's game'.

question: True or false: citizens of Monaco are forbidden by law from gambling in the famous Monte Carlo Casino.
source_excerpt: Citizens of Monaco are forbidden to enter the gaming rooms of the casino.

extra.why_interesting: The world's most glamorous casino is in a country whose own people are legally barred from the tables, the opposite of what a player would expect.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Monaco citizens are forbidden from entering the casino's gaming rooms, and I found no newer change to this.

explanation: The ban dates to the 19th century and was meant to keep the locals' money out of the casino while foreigners' money poured in.

question: During World War Two, British intelligence smuggled silk maps, compasses and real banknotes to prisoners of war hidden inside special editions of which board game?
source_excerpt: the British Secret Service contacted Waddingtons, as the company could also print on silk, to make Monopoly sets that included escape maps, money, a compass and file

extra.why_interesting: A family board game about buying property doubled as a covert escape kit, and the fake money in the box hid real money.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Waddingtons made Monopoly sets for the British Secret Service with silk escape maps, compasses and real money hidden inside, sent to POWs.

explanation: The sets were made by the British manufacturer Waddingtons and delivered through fake charities, with real currency tucked beneath the game's play money.

question: The board game Trivial Pursuit was invented in 1979 by two journalists from which country?
source_excerpt: Chris Haney, a photo editor for Montreal's The Gazette, and Scott Abbott, a sports editor for The Canadian Press

extra.why_interesting: The quintessential quiz-night board game feels American or British, but it was dreamed up over a game of Scrabble by two Canadian newspapermen.
extra.verification_notes: Trivial Pursuit was invented 15 Dec 1979 by Canadians Chris Haney (photo editor) and Scott Abbott (sports editor), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trivial_Pursuit.

explanation: Chris Haney and Scott Abbott came up with the idea in Montreal after finding pieces missing from their Scrabble set, and it went on to sell tens of millions of copies.

question: The doubling cube in backgammon shows 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 on five of its faces. What number is on the sixth?
source_excerpt: with the numbers 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 inscribed on its sides to denote the current stake

extra.why_interesting: You don't need to have played backgammon: once you hear the doubling pattern, the missing face is pure reasoning.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Doubling cube article lists the faces as 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64, so 64 is correct.

explanation: Each face doubles the stakes again, so the sixth face reads 64, though games that actually reach it are vanishingly rare.

question: Colonel Mustard, Miss Scarlett and Professor Plum are suspects in which classic murder-mystery board game?
source_excerpt: The classic suspects include Colonel Mustard, Miss Scarlett, and Professor Plum.

extra.why_interesting: An easy, warm recognition hit: the colourful suspect names are instantly familiar even to people who haven't played in decades.
extra.verification_notes: Mustard, Scarlett and Plum are classic suspects in Cluedo (Clue in North America); the 2016 and 2023 character changes did not affect them.

explanation: The game was invented in England during the Second World War and is sold as Clue in North America, with the lead pipe, candlestick and revolver among its six weapons.

question: In which hugely popular 1995 board game do players build settlements on hexagonal tiles while trading wood, brick, sheep, wheat and ore?
source_excerpt: The game was rebranded to simply "Catan" in 2015 for its 20th anniversary; released 1995 in Germany as The Settlers of Catan.

extra.why_interesting: The list of resources is unmistakable to anyone who has ever shouted 'anyone got sheep?' across a table, and it sparked the modern board-game boom.
extra.verification_notes: Catan (originally The Settlers of Catan, 1995, renamed Catan in 2015) matches the question; no newer development invalidates it, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catan

explanation: Designed by Klaus Teuber in Germany, The Settlers of Catan has sold tens of millions of copies and is widely credited with launching the modern board-game revival.

question: On a standard six-sided die, the dots on any two opposite faces always add up to the same number. What is it?
source_excerpt: Opposite sides of a modern die traditionally add up to seven

extra.why_interesting: Players have rolled dice all their lives without noticing there is a fixed rule to how the dots are arranged; once stated, they can reconstruct it from the pairs 1–6, 2–5, 3–4.
extra.verification_notes: Opposite faces of a standard modern die sum to seven per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dice; no newer developments could change this.

explanation: The faces are paired one with six, two with five, and three with four, so whichever face is up, the hidden bottom face brings the total to seven.

question: In 1904, Lizzie Magie patented The Landlord's Game to warn people about the evils of hoarding property. Which famous board game grew out of it?
source_excerpt: granted in 1904

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes the world's most famous celebration of ruthless property-grabbing was designed to glorify it; in fact it began as a protest against exactly that, invented by a woman two decades before the Depression-era version.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the patent was granted in 1904 and that The Landlord's Game evolved into Monopoly.

explanation: Magie wanted to show how landlords enrich themselves at everyone else's expense, but decades later the game was reworked and sold as Monopoly, celebrating the very behaviour she was warning against.

question: Many deep-sea shrimp and fish are bright red, yet they live in near-total darkness where being spotted means being eaten. Why does a red body actually make them almost invisible down there?
correct_answer: Red light never reaches the depths
alternative_answers: Red appears black in the deep sea
No red light at depth, so nothing is reflected
Red absorbs the blue bioluminescent light
Red is invisible without red light
headline_answer: Red light never reaches the depths
source_excerpt: Red light is quickly filtered from water as depth increases, so red animals in deep water appear black and are essentially invisible.

extra.verification_notes: Standard accepted explanation: red light is filtered out of seawater at depth, so red animals appear black and invisible to most predators (https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/ocean-fact/animal-color/).

explanation: Water absorbs the long red wavelengths of sunlight first, within the top few dozen metres, while blue light penetrates far deeper. In the deep sea there is essentially no red light left to reflect, so a red animal reflects nothing and appears black against the darkness. Red pigment is also cheaper for the body to make than true black melanin, and it even hides the glow of bioluminescent prey in a shrimp's stomach. Most deep-sea bioluminescence is blue, which red skin absorbs rather than reflects, so a predator's blue searchlight reveals nothing.

question: The biggest fish in the ocean can grow longer than a bus, yet it feeds almost entirely on plankton. What is it?
source_excerpt: the largest known extant fish species

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the biggest fish must be a fearsome hunter; the ocean's largest fish is a gentle plankton-sieving giant.
extra.verification_notes: Whale shark is the largest extant fish (up to ~18.8 m, longer than a ~12 m bus) and a filter feeder on plankton; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Each whale shark carries a unique pattern of spots, and researchers identify individuals with software originally built to match star fields in astronomy photos.

question: The narwhal's spiral 'horn' can reach 3 metres long. It is in fact an overgrown version of which ordinary body part?
source_excerpt: a long, spiralled tusk, which is a canine tooth that projects from the left side of the upper jaw

extra.why_interesting: The 'unicorn horn' image is so strong that players rarely stop to ask what the spike actually is: a single enormous tooth.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the narwhal tusk is an elongated left upper canine tooth reaching up to about 3 m.

explanation: It is the upper left canine, grown straight out through the lip, and it is packed with nerve endings, so the narwhal can likely sense water temperature and salinity with it.

question: Despite what its common name suggests, the killer whale is actually the largest member of which family of marine mammals?
source_excerpt: The orca (Orcinus orca), or killer whale, is a toothed whale and the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family.

extra.why_interesting: The word 'whale' in the name hides the fact that the ocean's apex predator is a very large, very clever relative of Flipper.
extra.verification_notes: Orca is the largest oceanic dolphin (Delphinidae); any taxonomic splitting of the orca would not change its family.

explanation: Orcas are oceanic dolphins, and a big male can top 9 metres and six tonnes, which makes it a dolphin heavier than an elephant.

question: True or false: the polar bear is officially classified as a marine mammal.
source_excerpt: They include animals such as cetaceans, pinnipeds, sirenians, marine otters, sea otters and polar bears.

extra.why_interesting: A furry bear that walks on four legs feels like the opposite of a whale, yet biologists and the law file it with the marine mammals.
extra.verification_notes: Polar bears are classified as marine mammals (e.g., under the US Marine Mammal Protection Act and in standard marine mammal lists) per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_mammal.

explanation: True: it spends most of its life on sea ice hunting seals, so it is grouped with whales, seals and sea otters as a marine mammal, and the US Marine Mammal Protection Act covers it.

question: In 2016 scientists dated the eye lenses of an Arctic species and estimated one female was around 400 years old, the longest-lived vertebrate ever recorded. Which animal?
source_excerpt: Greenland sharks have the longest lifespan of any known vertebrate, estimated to be between 272 and 510 years.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the oldest backboned animal to be a tortoise or a whale; it is a slow, half-blind shark that may predate the founding of many modern nations.
extra.verification_notes: The 2016 Science study (Nielsen et al.) dated a Greenland shark at about 392±120 years, the longest-lived vertebrate known, and no newer record overtakes it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland_shark).

explanation: Greenland sharks grow about a centimetre a year and are thought not to reach sexual maturity until roughly 150 years old.

question: Genetic studies show the closest living relatives of whales and dolphins are not seals or any other sea creature, but a large African land mammal. Which one?
source_excerpt: the closest living relatives of the hippopotamids are cetaceans (whales, dolphins, porpoises, etc.), from which they diverged about 55 million years ago.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for seals or manatees; the real nearest cousin is a land-dwelling, grass-eating African heavyweight.
extra.verification_notes: Hippos (family Hippopotamidae) are the closest living relatives of cetaceans, per Wikipedia's Hippopotamus article; no newer findings contradict this.

explanation: Whales and hippos share a common ancestor from around 55 million years ago, and both still rely on underwater sound for communication.

question: In its first months, a blue whale calf drinking its mother's milk gains roughly how much weight every day?
source_excerpt: Nursing blue whale calves gain 90 kg (200 lbs.) each day.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows blue whales are huge, but few grasp the rate: a calf puts on the weight of an adult human every single day.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources, including SeaWorld, state blue whale calves gain about 90 kg (200 lb) per day on milk; no contradicting authority found.

explanation: Around 90 kilograms a day, roughly an adult human's weight, fuelled by hundreds of litres of milk that is about half fat.

question: Jelly-filled pores on a shark's snout, called the ampullae of Lorenzini, let it find prey buried in sand by sensing what?
source_excerpt: electroreceptive fish may pick up weak electrical stimuli from the muscle contractions of their prey

extra.why_interesting: Players think of sharks as smell machines; the twist is a sixth sense, reading the faint electricity of a buried fish's heartbeat.
extra.verification_notes: Ampullae of Lorenzini are gel-filled electroreceptors that detect electric fields, including those from hidden prey; secondary roles (magnetic or temperature sensing) don't make the answer wrong.

explanation: Every living muscle and nerve gives off tiny electrical signals, and sharks can pick up even the heartbeat of a flatfish hidden under the seabed.

question: Two-metre-long tube worms clustered around deep-sea hot vents have no mouth and no gut. What keeps them fed?
source_excerpt: Adult Riftia worms lack a digestive system and rely on their symbiotic relationship with chemotrophic sulfur-oxidising bacteria

extra.why_interesting: An animal with no mouth and no gut sounds impossible; the answer reveals a whole food chain running on volcanic chemicals instead of sunlight.
extra.verification_notes: Riftia pachyptila adults lack a mouth and gut and are nourished by chemosynthetic symbiotic bacteria in the trophosome; the 2 m length is consistent with sizes up to 3 m (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riftia_pachyptila).

explanation: Bacteria living inside the worm turn hydrogen sulfide from the vent water into food, an ecosystem that runs with no sunlight at all.

question: Which marine mammal has no blubber at all, and instead keeps warm with the densest fur in the animal kingdom?
source_excerpt: Unlike most other marine mammals, the sea otter has no blubber and relies on its exceptionally thick fur to keep warm.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every sea mammal is wrapped in fat; this one survives cold Pacific water with fur alone, which is why oil spills are so deadly to it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms sea otters have no blubber and the densest fur of any animal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_otter).

explanation: A sea otter packs over 100,000 hairs into a single square centimetre, and it must groom constantly, because if the fur gets matted it loses its insulation and the animal can die of cold.

question: Ambergris, a waxy lump that perfumers have paid more than its weight in gold for, forms in the intestines of which whale species?
source_excerpt: Ambergris is formed from a secretion of the bile duct in the intestines of the sperm whale.

extra.why_interesting: A luxury perfume ingredient turns out to be a lump that formed in the gut of a whale, and the species is the one with the giant square head.
extra.verification_notes: Ambergris is produced only by sperm whales, forming in the intestines; the gold-price comparison is only flavor text and doesn't affect the answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambergris).

explanation: It is thought to build up around indigestible squid beaks, and beachcombers still occasionally find chunks worth tens of thousands of euros.

question: The megamouth, a shark that grows to over 5 metres, was completely unknown to science until one got tangled in a US Navy ship's sea anchor off Hawaii. In which year?
source_excerpt: The initial specimen was captured on November 15, 1976, approximately 25 miles northeast of Kahuku, Hawaii... entangled in the sea anchor of the USS AFB-14

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a 5-metre shark must have been catalogued in the age of sailing ships; it stayed unknown until the era of disco.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the first megamouth was caught in the sea anchor of USS AFB-14 off Hawaii on 15 Nov 1976, and no later discovery displaces this.

explanation: It happened in 1976, and the species was so unlike anything known that it needed its own new family; fewer than a few hundred have ever been seen since.

question: In 2014 a tagged whale was recorded nearly 3 kilometres below the surface, the deepest dive ever measured for any mammal. It was not a sperm whale. Which species was it?
source_excerpt: included dives to 2992 m depth and lasting 137.5 min, both new mammalian dive records.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone's guess is the sperm whale; the real record holder is a shy, little-known whale that beats it by hundreds of metres.
extra.verification_notes: Schorr et al. 2014 (PLOS ONE) recorded a Cuvier's beaked whale dive to 2,992 m, a mammal depth record, and I found no later record that beats it.

explanation: Cuvier's beaked whales also hold the breath-holding record, with one dive timed at over three and a half hours.

question: Which jawless, eel-shaped seabed scavenger defends itself by turning the surrounding water into a thick gel of slime within seconds, enough to choke an attacking shark?
source_excerpt: When released in seawater, the slime expands to 10,000 times its original size in 0.4 seconds.

extra.why_interesting: Ink and spines are the defences people expect; this animal fights off sharks by turning the water itself into a choking gel.
extra.verification_notes: Hagfish are eel-shaped jawless scavengers whose slime gels in seawater in under a second and clogs predators' gills, per Wikipedia.

explanation: A single hagfish can gel a whole bucket of water almost instantly, then wipes itself clean by tying its body in a knot and sliding the knot down its length.

question: Biologists fear that warming beaches could doom some sea turtle populations, even though the adults are healthy, lay plenty of eggs, and the eggs still hatch normally. Why would warmer sand be a threat?
correct_answer: Warmer sand produces almost only females
alternative_answers: Too many females, not enough males
Hot nests skew the sex ratio
No males will be born to breed
Sand temperature decides whether hatchlings are male or female
headline_answer: Warmer sand produces almost only females
source_excerpt: a nest just one or two degrees warmer may yield nearly all females, and cooler sand brings more males.

extra.verification_notes: Sea turtle temperature-dependent sex determination means warmer sand yields female-biased hatchlings, raising population viability concerns (https://marinelife.org/heat-waves-are-shaping-the-future-of-sea-turtle-populations/).

explanation: Sea turtles have temperature-dependent sex determination: the sex of a hatchling is set by the temperature of the sand during incubation, not by genes. Cooler nests produce mostly males and warmer nests mostly females, with the switch happening within a narrow band of about one degree. As beaches heat up, some rookeries are already producing over 99 percent female hatchlings. The population looks healthy for decades because the females keep nesting, but with almost no males being born, there will eventually be too few mates and fertile eggs for the population to sustain itself.

question: In which country would you find the world's largest living lizard roaming in the wild?
source_excerpt: the largest extant species of lizard... endemic to the Indonesian islands of Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Dasami, and Gili Motang

extra.why_interesting: Players know the name 'Komodo dragon' but often can't place Komodo on a map; the question rewards connecting the famous animal to its one home country.
extra.verification_notes: The Komodo dragon is the largest extant lizard and is endemic to Indonesia, so the answer holds; I found nothing newer that overturns it.

explanation: The Komodo dragon lives only on a few Indonesian islands such as Komodo, Rinca and Flores, where adults can top three metres and ambush deer and even water buffalo.

question: A snake constantly flicks its forked tongue in and out. Which sense is it mainly using that tongue for?
source_excerpt: They collect particles from the air, ground, or water using their forked tongue, which are then transferred to the vomeronasal organ (also known as Jacobson's organ) in the mouth for analysis.

extra.why_interesting: Many people assume the flicking is a threat or a way of tasting; the real answer is that the snake is sniffing the air with its tongue.
extra.verification_notes: Snake tongue flicking delivers chemical particles to the vomeronasal organ, which Wikipedia describes as smell, though some sources call it combined taste-smell. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake

explanation: The tongue collects scent particles and presses them against the Jacobson's organ in the roof of the mouth, so a snake effectively smells in stereo with its tongue.

question: Which egg-laying mammal's males carry a venomous spur on their hind legs?
source_excerpt: The spurs of the male inject venom, which is powerful enough to inflict pain in humans.

extra.why_interesting: People know the platypus is weird for laying eggs and having a duck bill, but far fewer know the males are also venomous.
extra.verification_notes: Male platypuses have venomous hind-leg spurs; echidna spurs are non-venomous, so the answer is unique (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus).

explanation: On top of its duck bill and egg-laying, the male platypus delivers venom through a spur on each hind ankle, painful enough to leave a human in agony for days.

question: Males of this species can pass six metres in length and are found from eastern India to northern Australia. What is the largest living reptile?
source_excerpt: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile.

extra.why_interesting: Players tend to say 'crocodile' and stop; the fun is knowing which crocodile, and that it ranges across salt water from India to northern Australia.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile, with males reaching about 6 m and rarely exceeding 6.3 m, ranging from eastern India to northern Australia.

explanation: The saltwater or estuarine crocodile is the biggest reptile alive today, with the largest males weighing around a tonne and happily swimming far out to sea between islands.

question: The axolotl, the salamander that keeps its feathery gills for life, survives in the wild only in canals on the edge of which capital city?
source_excerpt: native to the freshwater lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco in the Valley of Mexico

extra.why_interesting: The axolotl is a pet-shop and internet celebrity, yet almost nobody realises its entire wild range is a few canals inside one of the biggest cities on Earth.
extra.verification_notes: Wild axolotls survive only in the Xochimilco canals in Mexico City, and they keep their external gills for life; no newer development contradicts this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axolotl).

explanation: Wild axolotls cling on only in the Xochimilco canals of Mexico City, where pollution and introduced fish have pushed them to the brink even as millions live in labs and aquariums worldwide.

question: When cornered by a coyote, the North American horned lizard squirts a stream of something from the corners of its eyes. What?
source_excerpt: The blood not only confuses predators but also tastes foul to canine and feline predators.

extra.why_interesting: The player expects venom or a foul liquid; the truth that the lizard fires its own blood from its eyes is stranger than any guess.
extra.verification_notes: Horned lizards squirt blood from the eyes to deter canine predators such as coyotes, per Wikipedia's Phrynosoma article.

explanation: The lizard raises the blood pressure in its head until vessels around the eyes burst, firing blood up to a metre or more, and the foul taste sends dogs and coyotes packing.

question: Which blind, pale salamander of the caves of Slovenia and Croatia is nicknamed the 'human fish' and can go years without eating?
source_excerpt: an olm can survive up to 10 years without food.

extra.why_interesting: Central European players may know the animal as a national symbol; others are startled that a salamander lives its whole life blind in the dark and can skip meals for years.
extra.verification_notes: Olm (Proteus) is the 'human fish' of Slovenian/Croatian caves, blind, pale and able to survive about 10 years without food; the 2026 split into nine species doesn't change the common name.

explanation: The olm, or proteus, lives its whole life in pitch-dark cave rivers, has skin the colour of a pale human arm, and in lab conditions has survived around a decade with no food at all.

question: Nicknamed the 'water bear', which microscopic eight-legged animal survived being exposed to the vacuum of open space in a 2007 experiment?
source_excerpt: A landmark 2007 experiment aboard the FOTON-M3 mission exposed tardigrades to the vacuum of space and ultraviolet radiation for 10 days.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume nothing survives naked exposure to space; the answer is a tiny eight-legged animal most people have never seen with their own eyes.
extra.verification_notes: Tardigrades ('water bears') survived vacuum exposure on the 2007 FOTON-M3 mission, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrade; I found no newer event that changes this.

explanation: Tardigrades dry themselves into a shrunken 'tun' state that shrugs off vacuum, radiation and freezing, and some of the 2007 space travellers went on to lay viable eggs afterwards.

question: Three of these animals are amphibians. Which one is a reptile?
source_excerpt: Skinks are lizards that constitute the family Scincidae

extra.why_interesting: All four names sound like obscure creepy-crawlies, so the player must actually know that a caecilian is a legless amphibian while a skink is a lizard.
extra.verification_notes: Skinks are lizards (reptiles); newts, caecilians and salamanders are amphibians, so the answer is unique and correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skink).

explanation: The skink is a lizard, so a reptile, while the caecilian, despite looking like a giant worm with no legs at all, is a true amphibian alongside the newt and salamander.

question: The leatherback is the largest sea turtle and a champion diver. Roughly how deep has a leatherback been recorded diving?
source_excerpt: Individuals have been recorded diving to depths as great as 1,280 m (4,200 ft).

extra.why_interesting: Players picture turtles paddling near the surface; realising a reptile that breathes air dives more than a kilometre down reframes the whole animal.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia reports a leatherback recorded diving to 1,280 m, so 'About 1,000 metres' is the closest option; the other options are clearly wrong.

explanation: Tracking tags have recorded a leatherback at around 1,280 metres, deep into cold, crushing darkness, hunting jellyfish on a single breath.

question: A hormone found in the saliva of which venomous lizard of the American Southwest became the basis of a widely prescribed diabetes drug?
source_excerpt: In 1992, researcher John Eng isolated a novel substance from Gila monster venom which he called exendin-4.

extra.why_interesting: Nobody expects a diabetes medicine to come from a venomous desert lizard; players who know the Gila monster is one of the few venomous lizards can reason their way there.
extra.verification_notes: Exenatide was derived from exendin-4, isolated from Gila monster saliva/venom by John Eng (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exenatide).

explanation: The Gila monster's saliva contains exendin-4, and its synthetic copy exenatide helps type 2 diabetics control blood sugar, a payoff from a lizard that eats only a few big meals a year.

question: Which flat South American toad, named after a former Dutch colony, raises its young inside pockets in the skin of the mother's back?
source_excerpt: eggs on their backs, in honeycomb-like depressions directly within the skin, releasing fully-formed froglets after a period of 4–5 months

extra.why_interesting: Most players know frogs lay eggs in water; the image of babies hatching out of holes in their mother's back is unforgettable, and the country name in the toad's name gives a foothold.
extra.verification_notes: Pipa pipa, the Surinam toad (Suriname was Dutch), carries eggs embedded in skin of the female's back; no ambiguity found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surinam_toad).

explanation: After mating, the eggs sink into the female's back skin and seal over, and months later tiny fully formed toadlets pop out of the honeycomb of holes.

question: Jonathan, a giant tortoise living on the island of St Helena, is the oldest known living land animal. In roughly which decade did he hatch?
source_excerpt: Jonathan, born approximately 1832, is the oldest known living land animal.

extra.why_interesting: Players know tortoises live long, but a living animal that hatched before the first photograph was taken stretches belief; the options let them estimate rather than recall.
extra.verification_notes: Jonathan is still alive and was hatched around 1832, so 1830s is correct; I found no newer record holder or death (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_(tortoise)).

explanation: Jonathan is thought to have hatched around 1832 and was already fully grown when he arrived on St Helena in 1882, so he has lived through the entire history of photography and the motor car.

question: In a famous Stanford experiment on self-control, small children were left alone with one treat and told they could have two if they waited about fifteen minutes. Which sweet gave the test its name?
topic: The human mind: memory, illusions and psychology
source_excerpt: Wait time: 15 minutes; one preferred treat immediately OR a second treat if they waited (Marshmallows and pretzel sticks)

extra.why_interesting: Players know 'the test about kids and willpower' but the sweet itself is the hook; the payoff is that the follow-up studies claimed the patient kids did better decades later.
extra.verification_notes: The test is universally known as the Stanford marshmallow experiment, with a ~15-minute wait for a second treat, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_marshmallow_experiment.

explanation: Walter Mischel's marshmallow test became famous when later follow-ups suggested the children who waited went on to do better in school and life, though newer studies have softened that claim.

question: In 1956, psychologist George Miller published a paper on how many separate items we can hold in short-term memory at once, calling it the 'magical number', plus or minus two. Which number?
topic: The human mind: memory, illusions and psychology
source_excerpt: often interpreted to argue that the number of objects an average human can hold in short-term memory is 7 ± 2

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has felt the limit when juggling a phone number in their head; putting a precise, famous number on it is satisfying.
extra.verification_notes: Miller's 1956 Psychological Review paper is titled 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two', so seven is correct; later work suggesting about four chunks doesn't change what the paper claimed.

explanation: Miller's paper is one of the most cited in psychology, and it is why phone numbers and chunked codes tend to hover around seven digits.

question: Each of your eyes has a small patch with no light-sensitive cells at all, a hole in your vision that your brain quietly paints over. What leaves the eyeball at that exact spot?
topic: The human mind: memory, illusions and psychology
source_excerpt: The optic disc or optic nerve head is the point of exit for ganglion cell axons leaving the eye.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume their field of vision is complete; learning there is a permanent hole the brain paints over is a small shock.
extra.verification_notes: The blind spot is the optic disc, where retinal ganglion cell axons exit the eye as the optic nerve; retinal veins also exit there, but the optic nerve is the canonical answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optic_disc).
